The biggest tradeoff is between **lower housing costs and faster growth in Austin and Raleigh** versus **New York’s much stronger transit orientation and larger scale**.

Austin and Raleigh have similar 2024 median household incomes—$100,431 in Austin and $100,103 in Raleigh—but Raleigh is more affordable on the supplied housing measures. Its median rent was $1,573 versus Austin’s $1,726, and its median home value was $418,400 versus $465,000. Housing costs also represented a smaller share of income in Raleigh: 18.9% for rent and a 4.2 home-value-to-income ratio, compared with 20.6% and 4.6% in Austin.

New York had a slightly lower median household income of $99,155 and the highest housing costs: $1,830 median rent, a $614,200 median home value, and a 6.2 home-value-to-income ratio. Its poverty rate was also higher at 12.7%, compared with 9.8% in Austin and 8.7% in Raleigh.

Austin and Raleigh are the faster-growing metros. From 2020 to 2025, Austin’s population grew 13.9% and Raleigh’s 12.6%, while New York’s grew 0.6%. The 2023 migration figures show positive net migration for Austin (+18,309) and Raleigh (+14,044), but negative net migration for New York (-120,800). These figures describe different periods from the 2025 population estimates, so they should not be treated as simultaneous measures.

Transportation differs sharply. New York had a 24.1% transit commuting share and a 44.6% drive share, compared with transit shares of 1.1% in Austin and 0.5% in Raleigh. Austin had the highest work-from-home share at 26.8%, narrowly ahead of Raleigh’s 26.2% and well above New York’s 16.7%. Average commute time was shortest in Raleigh at 26.8 minutes, followed closely by Austin at 27.3 minutes; New York’s was 35.6 minutes.

Educational attainment is broadly similar between Austin and Raleigh, with bachelor’s-degree-or-higher shares of 50.9% and 51.2%, respectively. New York’s was lower at 44.2%, while its high-school-or-higher share was also lower: 87.6% versus 91.9% in Austin and 93.2% in Raleigh.

In short, **Raleigh offers the lowest housing costs among these options, Austin combines strong growth with somewhat higher housing costs, and New York stands apart for scale and transit use but has higher housing costs, longer commutes, and much weaker recent net migration**.
